title: In curated mouse knockouts, 21 of 77 lncRNA genes had a phenotype like the nearest gene's knockout, 2.7 times the gene-pair rate, mostly lncRNAs named after that gene
abstract:
In the mouse knockout record, the defects of mice that lose a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) gene resemble those of mice that lose the nearest protein-coding gene about 2.7 times more often than in pairs of neighbouring protein-coding genes, and the excess comes mostly from lncRNAs named after that neighbour. This matters because papers often use a lncRNA knockout defect as evidence that the RNA itself has a function; a defect that copies the neighbour's defect is also consistent with an effect on the neighbouring gene, or with investigators looking first for the neighbour's phenotype.

We used all single-gene mouse genotypes with curated phenotypes in Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI, November 2026). For each locus we measured how similar its knockout phenotype is to that of its nearest protein-coding gene (information-weighted overlap of Mammalian Phenotype ontology terms) and ranked this similarity against protein-coding genes with equally rich records; 'copying' means the neighbour ranks in the top 5%. With annotations from single-locus studies and no shared papers, 21 of 77 lncRNA genes copied (27.3%, 95% CI 18.6-38.1%), against 8.8% for 1,950 neighbouring gene pairs (10.0% after reweighting; Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio 3.4, 2.0-5.8). Enhancers and other regulatory elements copied at 33%. The excess held in eleven sensitivity analyses, including removal of loci within 2 kb of the gene and a required specific shared term.

The pattern fits ascertainment at least as well as local regulation. lncRNAs named after their neighbour copied in 13 of 28 cases (46%), the other 49 in 8 (16%; not significantly above baseline, p = 0.07). MicroRNA genes inside protein-coding genes, whose products act elsewhere, copied their host as often as lncRNAs did (26%), and protein-coding genes next to the same neighbours copied at 20%. Distance and allele design did not separate the explanations, although at Hand2os1 and Lncenc1 only the polyA-insertion alleles copied. The systematic IMPC pipeline cannot test ascertainment, because its gene pairs copy at chance level. We give a locus table and laboratory tests, including a cis-trans test.

display.caption: a: Fraction of loci whose knockout phenotype is in the top 5% of similarity to the knockout phenotype of the nearest protein-coding gene (matched analysis; 95% Wilson intervals), with the gene-pair baseline (dashed, 8.8%) and chance (dotted). microRNA genes inside protein-coding genes copy their host as often as lncRNAs copy their neighbour. b: Other lncRNA genes (orange) and protein-coding gene pairs (blue) in ten analysis variants; the excess is absent only for the second-nearest gene.

a: Copying by naming: lncRNAs named after their neighbour copy far more often than other lncRNAs; protein-coding genes next to the same neighbours (same-neighbour control) copy at 20%. b: Copying by position relative to the nearest gene (exploratory; no distance trend).

Copying by lncRNA allele design (other lncRNA genes, single-locus alleles, gene level) and by how the mouse line was made (allele level). Designs do not differ significantly. The 11 IMPC/KOMP lines do not copy, but IMPC-scored gene pairs copy only at chance level, so this check has no power.
